title: Celsus sidesteps the argument from prophecy
source_text: Εἶτα μετὰ ταῦτα, βουλόμενος ἀνατρέπειν τὴν πίστιν τῶν διὰ τὸ πεπροφητεῦσθαι παραδεξαμένων τὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, φησί· φέρε ἐὰν προείπωσιν οἱ προφῆται τὸν μέγαν θεὸν, ἵνα μηδὲν ἄλλο φορτικώτερον εἴπω, δουλεύειν ἢ νοσήσειν ἢ ἀποθανεῖν, τεθνήξεσθαι δεήσει τὸν θεὸν ἢ δουλεύειν ἢ νοσήσειν. ἐπειδὴ προείρητο, ἵνα πιστευθῇ ἀποθανὼν ὅτι θεὸς ἦν; ἀλλ᾿ οὐκ ἂν προείποιεν τοῦτο οἱ προφῆται· κακὸν γάρ ἐστι καὶ ἀνόσιον. οὐκοῦν οὔτ᾿ εἰ προεῖπον οὔτ᾿ εἰ μὴ προεῖπον. σκεπτέον, ἀλλ᾿ εἰ τὸ ἔργον ἄξιόν ἐστι θεοῦ καὶ καλόν. τῷ δ᾿ αἰσχρῷ καὶ κακῷ, κἂν πάντες ἄνθρωποι μαινόμενοι προλέγειν δοκῶσιν, ἀπιστητέον. πῶς οὖν τὰ περὶ τοῦτον ὡς περὶ θεὸν πραχθέντα ἐστὶν ὅσια; φαίνεται δὴ διὰ τούτων ἰσχυρὸν μέν τι πρὸς πειθὼ τῶν ἀκουόντων ὑπονενοηκέναι τὸ περὶ τοῦ πεπροφητεῦσθαι τὸν Ἰησοῦν κεφάλαιον. ἄλλῳ δὲ πιθανῷ πειρᾶσθαι ἀνατρέπειν τὸν λόγον φάσκων· οὐκοῦν οὔτ᾿ εἰ προεῖπον οὔτ᾿ εἰ μὴ προεῖπον, σκεπτέον. ἐχρῆν δ᾿, εἴπερ μὴ παραλογιστικῶς ἀλλ᾿ ἀποδεικτικῶς ἐβούλετο ἐνστῆναι τῷ λεγομένῳ, εἰπεῖν· οὐκοῦν ἀποδεικτέον ὅτι οὐ προεῖπον ἢ οὐ, καθὼς προεῖπον, τὰ περὶ Χριστοῦ πεπλήρωται ἐν τῷ Ἰησοῦ λεχθέντα. καὶ ἐπιφέρειν τὴν δοκοῦσαν αὐτῷ ἀπόδειξιν. οὕτως γὰρ ἐφαίνετο ἂν, τίνα μὲν αἱ προφητεῖαι λέγουσιν ὑφ᾿ ἡμῶν ἀναφερόμενα ἐπὶ τὸν Ἰησοῦν, πῶς δὲ οὗτος ψευδοποιεῖ τὴν ἐκδοχὴν ἡμῶν· καὶ εὑρέθη ἂν, πότερον γενναίως ἀνατρέπει τὰ ὑφ᾿ ἡμῶν φερόμενα ἀπὸ τῶν προφητῶν εἰς τὸν περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ λόγον, ἢ ἁλίσκεται ἀναισχύντως βιάζεσθαι θέλων τὴν τῆς ἀληθείας ἐνάργειαν ὡς οὐκ ἀλήθειαν.
pass_a_gloss: Then after these things, wishing to overturn (ἀνατρέπω) the faith (πίστις) of those who accepted (παραδέχομαι) the things of Jesus through their having been prophesied (προφητεύω), he says: 'Come (φέρε), if the prophets foretold (προλέγω) the great God, that I may say nothing else more offensive (φορτικός), would be a slave (δουλεύω) or fall sick (νοσέω) or die (ἀποθνῄσκω), will it be necessary (δεῖ) for God to die or be a slave or fall sick, since it had been foretold, that having died he may be believed (πιστεύω) that he was God? But the prophets would not foretell this; for it is evil (κακός) and unholy (ἀνόσιος). So neither if they foretold nor if they did not foretell must be considered (σκεπτέον), but if the deed (ἔργον) is worthy (ἄξιος) of God and good (καλός). And the shameful (αἰσχρός) and evil must be disbelieved (ἀπιστητέον), even if all men raving (μαίνομαι) seem to foretell. How then are the things done (πράσσω) about this one as about God holy (ὅσιος)?' He appears through these things to have suspected (ὑπονοέω) the head-point (κεφάλαιον) about Jesus' having been prophesied to be something strong (ἰσχυρός) for persuasion (πειθώ) of the hearers, and by another plausible thing (πιθανόν) to try to overturn the argument (λόγος), saying: 'so neither if they foretold nor if they did not foretell must be considered.' But he ought, if not by fallacy (παραλογιστικῶς) but by demonstration (ἀποδεικτικῶς) he wished to oppose (ἐνίστημι) what is said, to say: 'so it must be demonstrated (ἀποδεικτέον) that they did not foretell, or that not as they foretold were the things said about Christ fulfilled (πληρόω) in Jesus', and to bring on (ἐπιφέρω) the demonstration (ἀπόδειξις) seeming so to him. For thus it would have appeared what the prophecies say which are referred (ἀναφέρω) by us to Jesus, and how he falsifies (ψευδοποιέω) our interpretation (ἐκδοχή); and it would have been found whether he nobly (γενναίως) overturns the things brought by us from the prophets into the account (λόγος) about Jesus, or is caught (ἁλίσκομαι) shamelessly (ἀναισχύντως) wishing to force (βιάζομαι) the clearness (ἐνάργεια) of the truth as not truth.
pass_b_english: Then, after this, wishing to overthrow the faith of those who have accepted what concerns Jesus because it had been prophesied, he says: “Come now: if the prophets foretold that the great God (to say nothing more offensive) would be a slave, or fall sick, or die, will it then be necessary for God to die, or be a slave, or fall sick, since it had been foretold, so that by dying he might be believed to be God? But the prophets would not foretell this, for it is evil and unholy. So we must not consider whether they foretold it or did not foretell it, but whether the deed is worthy of God and good. What is shameful and evil we must disbelieve, even if all men, gone mad, should seem to foretell it. How then can the things done in his case, as though he were God, be holy?”

Through these words he appears to have suspected that the point about Jesus’ having been prophesied was a strong one for persuading those who hear it, and to be trying to overturn the argument with another plausible point, saying: “So we must not consider whether they foretold it or did not foretell it.” But if he wished to object to the claim by demonstration and not by fallacy, he ought to have said: “So we must show that they did not foretell it, or that the things said about Christ were not fulfilled in Jesus as they foretold,” and then to have added what seemed to him a demonstration.

In that way it would have become clear what the prophecies say that we apply to Jesus, and how he proves our interpretation false; and it would have been found out whether he nobly overturns what we bring from the prophets in support of our account of Jesus, or whether he is caught shamelessly trying to force the clear evidence of the truth to pass for something that is not true.

choices.choice: The source punctuates οὐκοῦν οὔτ᾿ εἰ προεῖπον οὔτ᾿ εἰ μὴ προεῖπον. σκεπτέον with a full stop before σκεπτέον; Origen repeats the clause later with a comma, so the two are read as one sentence. ‘The great God’ and ‘God’ capitalised: Celsus means the supreme God, and the Christian claim that Jesus is God. τὰ περὶ τοῦτον πραχθέντα rendered ‘the things done in his case’ (not only things done to him). φαίνεται + infinitive (ὑπονενοηκέναι, πειρᾶσθαι) rendered ‘he appears to have’, not ‘it is plain that’. Origen’s proposed reply (‘So we must show...’) is put in quotation marks because the Greek frames it as words Celsus should have said; it is not a quotation of Celsus. No Scripture quoted.
φαίνεται + infinitive: 'it is plain that he suspected' (too strong) -> 'he appears to have suspected ... and to be trying'
τὰ περὶ τοῦτον ... πραχθέντα: 'the things done to this man, as though to God' -> 'the things done in his case, as though he were God' (περί is wider than 'to'; 'man' was added)
ἐνστῆναι τῷ λεγομένῳ: 'resist what is said' -> 'object to the claim'
Speaker check: Celsus's words (both the full quotation and Origen's repetition) in double quotes; Origen's model reply marked as what Celsus should have said
